points.title: Join definition
points.must: A query that combines rows from related tables by matching the foreign key with the primary key.

points.title: Join condition
points.must: WHERE Table1.FK = Table2.PK (or JOIN … ON …) — with the Titles / Publishers example.

points.title: Two ways to join
points.must: FROM A, B WHERE A.x = B.x and FROM A JOIN B ON A.x = B.x give the same result.

points.title: Steps for a two-table query
points.must: Fields as Table.field → both tables in FROM → join condition → extra conditions with AND → ORDER BY last.

points.title: Worked join example
points.must: A join with an extra condition and ORDER BY, plus its result table (e.g. books published in Almaty, cheapest first).

points.title: Missing join condition
points.must: Without it every row is paired with every row (5 × 3 = 15 rows) — a meaningless result.

points.title: Table.field and aliases
points.must: A field that exists in both tables must be written with the table name; aliases t, p.

points.title: Database with multiple tables
points.must: Data about different entities in separate tables linked by keys; each fact stored once, less redundancy.

points.title: Primary key vs foreign key
points.must: PK uniquely identifies records of its own table, never NULL; FK links to the PK of another table, can repeat.

points.title: Building the tables
points.must: From the ERD: tables, fields, PKs; FK in the 'many' table; same type as the PK; create parent tables first, then child tables; insert parents first.

points.title: CREATE TABLE with FOREIGN KEY
points.must: A full example: FOREIGN KEY (StudentID) REFERENCES Students(StudentID) in Loans.

points.title: Three-table query
points.must: A query with two join conditions (tables − 1), e.g. student name, book title, loan date.

points.title: Common mistakes
points.must: At least two: no join condition, ambiguous field names, wrong fields matched, child table created first, FK type different from PK.
